title: Making and working Egyptian blue – a review of the archaeological evidence
authors: Kovalev, I., Rodler, A.S., Broens, C., Rehren, T.
venue: Journal of Archaeological Science (accepted manuscript, Zenodo)
ask_addressed: Which of these are measured by archaeometry versus only described in texts?
quote: we note the absence of direct evidence for the production and processing of Egyptian blue for much of the known period of its use
summary: Review of published workshop evidence for Egyptian blue (a Ca-Cu silicate sintered at c. 850-1050 C, first attested c. 3100 BCE per the paper). Product analysis is abundant; direct production evidence is scarce and lacking for whole periods.
limits: Review of evidence for Egyptian blue only (Egypt plus wider Mediterranean/Near East), not green frit or other technologies. Opened as the author accepted manuscript via the Zenodo API file link; page 403s on the direct file URL.

title: Supplying the Mediterranean World with Egyptian blue: An Archaeometric Perspective
venue: Book chapter (Zenodo open-access copy; volume not stated on the file)
ask_addressed: Which of these are measured by archaeometry versus only described in texts?
quote: there is little information on the manufacture, the source of raw materials or trade of Egyptian blue
summary: Describes Egyptian blue as a sintered copper-calcium silicate and quotes Vitruvius (7.11.1) on the Puteoli recipe, set beside archaeometric work. Shows the split between a textual recipe (Roman) and what analysis can confirm.
limits: Focus is Graeco-Roman Mediterranean production, not pharaonic Egypt; Vitruvius is a 1st c. BCE textual description, not Kemet evidence.

title: The organic chemistry of embalming agents in Pharaonic and Graeco-Roman mummies
venue: Nature 413: 837-841 (White Rose repository record, abstract only)
ask_addressed: What chemical technologies is ancient Egypt (Kemet, Khemet) securely documented to have practised, from analysis of objects and texts: pigments (Egyptian blue, Egyptian green, frit), glass and faience, metallurgy (copper, gold, bronze), mummification materials (natron, resins, oils), cosmetics (galena, lead compounds, kohl), dyes, fermentation, medical recipes? Give dates and the kind of evidence (chemical analysis, texts, workshop remains).
quote: The nature of the organic treatments remains obscure, because the ancient Egyptians left no written record of the process.
summary: Frames mummification chemistry: natron as desiccant, organic preservatives needed, no native written record, only Herodotus and later Greek and Roman authors. Reports GC-MS study of dated mummy tissues, wrappings and resinous materials.
limits: Only the abstract record was opened (full text not available there), so the specific compounds and dates found are not cited here.

title: Complex organic chemical balms of Pharaonic animal mummies
authors: Buckley, S.A., Clark, K.A., Evershed, R.P.
venue: Nature 431: 294-299 (White Rose repository record, abstract only)
ask_addressed: What chemical technologies is ancient Egypt (Kemet, Khemet) securely documented to have practised, from analysis of objects and texts: pigments (Egyptian blue, Egyptian green, frit), glass and faience, metallurgy (copper, gold, bronze), mummification materials (natron, resins, oils), cosmetics (galena, lead compounds, kohl), dyes, fermentation, medical recipes? Give dates and the kind of evidence (chemical analysis, texts, workshop remains).
quote: fats, oils, beeswax, sugar gum, petroleum bitumen, and coniferous, Pistacia and possibly cedar resins
summary: Chemical analysis of Pharaonic cat, hawk and ibis mummies overturns the view that animals were only wrapped or dipped in resin.
limits: Abstract only; sample numbers and dating not read. Animal, not human, mummies.

title: Rethinking the Process of Animal Mummification in Ancient Egypt: Molecular Characterization of Embalming Material and the Use of Brassicaceae Seed Oil in the Mummification of Gazelle Mummies from Kom Mereh, Egypt
authors: Marković, M., Mezzatesta, E., Porcier, S., Vieillescazes, C., Mathe, C.
ask_addressed: Which of these are measured by archaeometry versus only described in texts?
quote: complex mixtures of plant oils, animal fats, conifer resin, and beeswax
summary: FT-IR and GC-MS of nine balm samples from six Roman-period gazelle mummies; also detects cruciferous seed oil, a use named in Pliny and 5th c. AD papyri but not previously shown in mummification.
limits: Roman period, animal mummies only. Identification of conifer resin is to family level.

title: Chemical characterization of embalming materials of four ibis mummies from the Musée des Confluences, Lyon
authors: Marković, M., Mezzatesta, E., Porcier, S., Vieillescazes, C., Mathe, C.
ask_addressed: Which of these are measured by archaeometry versus only described in texts?
quote: castor oil, beeswax and wood tar of a diterpenic resin belonging to the Pinaceae family
summary: FT-IR and GC-MS on balms from four votive ibis mummies. The introduction notes that Herodotus, Strabo and Pliny give scarce information on the organic substances used, so identification rests on chemistry.
limits: Small sample (four mummies); animal mummies; classical authors are late and vague about materials.

title: Recipes of Ancient Egyptian kohls more diverse than previously thought
authors: Riesmeier, M., Keute, J., Veall, M.-A., Borschneck, D., Stevenson, A., Garnett, A., Williams, A., Ragan, M., Devièse, T., et al.
ask_addressed: What chemical technologies is ancient Egypt (Kemet, Khemet) securely documented to have practised, from analysis of objects and texts: pigments (Egyptian blue, Egyptian green, frit), glass and faience, metallurgy (copper, gold, bronze), mummification materials (natron, resins, oils), cosmetics (galena, lead compounds, kohl), dyes, fermentation, medical recipes? Give dates and the kind of evidence (chemical analysis, texts, workshop remains).
quote: The presence of laurionite and phosgenite in Ancient Egyptian make-up likely stems from synthetic manufacture
summary: Multi-analytical study of 11 Petrie Museum kohl containers: galena and cerussite present; laurionite found in one and phosgenite in another, read as synthetic (citing Walter et al. 1999, which was not opened). Also finds manganese- and silicon-based and organic ingredients.
limits: Eleven objects only. The synthetic-origin claim is cited from earlier work, not newly proven here. The quote is the authors' inference (likely), not a measurement.

title: Simply red: A Late Bronze Age glass ingot from Amarna
ask_addressed: What chemical technologies is ancient Egypt (Kemet, Khemet) securely documented to have practised, from analysis of objects and texts: pigments (Egyptian blue, Egyptian green, frit), glass and faience, metallurgy (copper, gold, bronze), mummification materials (natron, resins, oils), cosmetics (galena, lead compounds, kohl), dyes, fermentation, medical recipes? Give dates and the kind of evidence (chemical analysis, texts, workshop remains).
quote: It is accepted that cobalt blue glass was manufactured at Amarna using a cobalt alum
summary: Analysis of an ingot from Amarna (Late Bronze Age, 14th c. BCE capital) places manufacture in Egypt and supports primary glass production there; background sets out cobalt-alum blue glass and copper colourants, with red glass at Ramesside Qantir.
limits: One ingot. The cobalt alum source (Kharga or Dakhla) is stated as probable. Date and Amarna origin partly rest on find context.
